blocks.heading: Real income per head
blocks.text:
Real income per head is price-adjusted income divided by the relevant population. It is also called real GDP per head (per capita): real GDP per head = real GDP ÷ population. Real GDP is nominal GDP adjusted for inflation, so real GDP per head shows the average quantity of goods and services available per person. The real adjustment removes the effect of price changes on the stated basis, while per head accounts for population size. These are separate steps. A higher real total can still give a lower per-person figure if population increases faster. Conversely, a country with a smaller total may have a larger average when its population is smaller. State the aggregate, price basis and population used.

A real income of N$120 million shared over 20,000 people gives N$6,000 per head. If the total becomes N$126 million with 21,000 people, the average remains N$6,000 despite the 5 percent total increase. This does not mean each person receives exactly N$6,000. It is an aggregate ratio, and different distributions can have the same mean. Income from unpaid or unrecorded activity and external costs may also be poorly represented by the chosen measure. Use the average as evidence about a dimension of resources, then examine distribution and other outcomes for a welfare judgement. The calculation is not a currency amount each household can claim or a guarantee that government provides the same sum. This links back to output in 7.3 and the comparison of indicators: a useful average has a precise scope and explicit limits. A per-head comparison also needs a consistent population boundary. An income total for one region divided by the population of another would have no clear meaning. Keep units compatible when totals are in millions, and label the average as money per person for the period rather than as a percentage.

The Human Development Index (HDI) combines health, education and income into a composite measure of human development. Its dimensions use life expectancy, years of schooling and income per head. Values lie between zero and one. A higher value indicates higher measured human development, but does not show every person’s living conditions or how income is distributed.

blocks.heading: Life expectancy
blocks.text:
Life expectancy at birth is the average years a newborn would live under the prevailing age-specific mortality conditions of the period. It is a summary of survival conditions, not the age every resident will reach or a prediction that future conditions remain unchanged. It also differs from the average age of all people currently living in the population.

For a living-standard comparison it provides information beyond monetary income, but it does not measure every part of health or wellbeing. A longer life can coexist with differences in disability, access, working conditions or experienced quality of life. A national average can also conceal group disparities. Use consistent definitions, periods and populations when comparing estimates, and do not infer an individual prognosis from a group statistic. The useful question is what dimension the indicator adds and what it leaves unmeasured. A comparison of 70 and 73 years would show different survival summaries on the stated basis, not that every resident gains three years from one isolated policy. Attributing a change to a specific cause needs further evidence about the conditions and other influences.

blocks.heading: Education and literacy
blocks.text:
Education indicators can concern access, participation, completion or attainment. Literacy measures concern relevant reading-and-writing skills under their stated definition. These measures are related but not interchangeable. More school places can expand opportunity, while attendance records participation and completion records a further stage. None alone describes the whole quality of learning or the skill of each individual. The population group and definition matter when interpreting a rate.

A region might increase school enrolment from 80 to 90 percent of a specified age group. The ten-percentage-point change is evidence of greater recorded participation on that basis, not proof of an equal increase in literacy. Teacher availability, resources and learners’ circumstances can influence what access produces. To investigate learning outcomes, obtain the relevant attainment or skill evidence rather than assume it from building numbers. Education can expand opportunities and productive capacity, but actual work also needs suitable demand and access. A literacy average may differ across ages or locations, so national results can conceal local needs. This links education to development and the digital divide: electronic resources can support learning if accessible and well used, while access alone does not prove attainment. A justified comparison states which stage is measured and uses additional indicators for the wider claim. Rates should identify the age group and skill criterion. An adult literacy rate and a school-enrolment rate use different populations and concepts, so their percentages cannot be ranked as though they were the same outcome. Each can add relevant evidence if interpreted on its own basis.

blocks.heading: Health, housing and sanitation
blocks.text:
Basic-living-condition indicators describe outcomes or access concerning health, housing and sanitation. A measure might report the proportion of a defined population with a specified service, or an outcome under a clear criterion. The definition is essential: a building count does not reveal whether residents can use it, a connection does not necessarily prove reliable service and an average may conceal an underserved group. State the population, criterion and period before comparing figures.

A settlement reporting 90 percent access to a sanitation arrangement has 10 percent outside that recorded coverage, but quality and reliability still need assessment. A housing measure may concern overcrowding, safety or access to essentials, each a different dimension. Health-service availability can be distinct from actual use or experienced outcomes. These examples show how indicators describe living conditions. Compare like definitions and identify who is excluded or constrained. A national average can improve while a particular remote area falls behind. This connects to the emphasis on distribution: a higher average is one fact, while the location and quality of the gain determine how people experience it. Use several relevant indicators rather than assume that a money figure or one infrastructure count answers every welfare question. A supported judgement identifies the observed improvement and the further evidence needed to assess meaningful access. An access improvement can be meaningful without resolving every limitation. State the dimension that improved and the group reached, then explain the remaining gap. This is more informative than either calling the entire population well served or dismissing the recorded gain because some residents still face a barrier. The evidence should retain that scope.
